title: Balance puzzles and the atoms of numbers
summary: Letters as labeled boxes, one-step equations as balance scales and inequalities as scales that stay tipped, then number theory opens: factors in pairs, the sieve, and primes as the atoms every number is built from.
materials: a hundred chart, printed or drawn once on graph paper
a small paper square and a hole punch to check the opener afterwards

problems.prompt: Fill the blank: 47 + ___ = 112.
explanation: The plus sentence hides a subtraction: the blank is whatever is left when 47 is taken away from 112.
Take 47 from 112 in two easy steps: 112 take 40 is 72, then take 7 more is 65.
Check forwards: 47 + 65 is 112. It closes.
problems.useAgain: when a sum gives you the total and one part, and the missing part falls out of undoing the plus.
hints: The two numbers on the left together make 112, and you already know one of them.
Undo the plus: one subtraction finds the blank.
problems.socraticHint: If both sides of a true plus sentence are equal, what happens to the sentence when you take 47 away from each side?

variant.prompt: Fill the blank: 38 + ___ = 104.

problems.prompt: Work out 6 x 99 in your head.
explanation: 99 is one step short of 100, and 100 is a friendly number.
Six 100s make 600, but that counts one extra for each of the six, so it is 6 too many.
600 take 6 is 594.
problems.useAgain: when a number sits just next to a friendly one, so you compute with the friendly one and repair the small difference.
hints: What friendly number is 99 hiding right next to?
If you use the friendly number instead, how much too big is your answer, exactly?
problems.socraticHint: What did each of the six 99s gain when you rounded it up, and where does that gain have to go at the end?

variant.prompt: Work out 7 x 99 in your head.

problems.prompt: Without working all three out fully, which of these is the biggest?
explanation: Use 25 x 8 as the anchor: quarters make it easy, 25 x 8 is 200.
24 x 9 is 24 x 8 plus one more 24: 192 + 24 is 216.
26 x 7 is 26 x 8 minus one 26: 208 take 26 is 182.
216 beats 200 beats 182, so 24 x 9 is the biggest.
problems.useAgain: when comparing products, and nudging each one to a nearby easy product settles the race without full multiplication.
hints: Find the one you can do instantly and use it as your measuring stick.
Turn each of the others into that easy one plus or minus a small repair.
problems.socraticHint: Each option trades a slightly bigger first number for a slightly smaller second one. Why does that trade not always come out even?

variant.prompt: Without working all three out fully, which of these is the biggest?

problems.prompt: A count by fives goes 40, 45, 50 and keeps climbing. What is the first number bigger than 62 that the count lands on?
explanation: Find the rule first: every number the count lands on ends in 0 or 5.
Walk up from 62: 63 no, 64 no, 65 ends in 5.
So 65 is the first landing spot past 62.
problems.useAgain: when a skip count has a fingerprint in its last digit, so you can spot its landing spots without counting from the start.
hints: Look at the last digit of every number the count lands on. What do they all share?
Climb from 62 one step at a time and check each last digit against the fingerprint.
problems.socraticHint: What do the last digits of all the multiples of 5 have in common, and why does that pattern never break?

variant.prompt: A count by fives goes 40, 45, 50 and keeps climbing. What is the first number bigger than 78 that the count lands on?

problem.prompt: Fold a paper square in half left over right, then in half again top over bottom, so it is a small square four layers thick. Punch one hole straight through the middle of the small square, through every layer, then unfold all the way. How many holes does the open sheet show? Answer in your head first; the real punch is for checking afterwards.
explanation: The punch does not know about folding. It just makes one hole in every layer of paper it passes through.
One fold doubles the layers, so two folds make 2 x 2, which is 4 layers under the punch.
Unfolding separates the layers again, and each layer carries its own hole to a different spot on the sheet.
Four layers, four holes, sitting in a symmetric little pattern around the middle.
problem.useAgain: when a fold-and-cut puzzle turns simple the moment you count layers instead of imagining the finished picture.
hints: Do not chase where the holes end up yet. First count the sheets of paper lying under the punch.
Each fold doubles the layers, and every layer under the punch gets its own hole.
problem.socraticHint: What does one fold do to the number of layers, and what does the punch do to every layer it meets?

variant.prompt: Fold a paper square in half just once, so it is two layers thick. Punch two holes through both layers, then unfold. How many holes does the open sheet show?

steps.title: The week's shape, honestly
steps.body: Most weeks the math lanes braid into the build. This week they do not, and that is on purpose, not an accident: no balance scale is hiding inside your soldering iron, and pretending one is would be a fake link. Balance puzzles and prime hunting are their own games, old and good ones, and today they get played for their own sake. The one thing the bench and the lanes do share this week is a habit: check the joint, check the answer, before you call it done.

problems.prompt: In math, a letter is a labeled box: b is a box holding a number you do not know yet. Every bag in a shop holds b buttons, the same number in each. You buy 3 full bags and find 2 loose buttons in your pocket. Which expression counts all your buttons?
explanation: The letter b is a box: whatever number is inside, each bag holds exactly that many.
Three bags hold b + b + b buttons, which is written 3b: three copies of the box.
The 2 loose buttons are not in any bag, so they are added as a plain 2.
Three copies of the box plus 2 loose is 3b + 2, whatever b turns out to be.
problems.useAgain: when a story mixes copies of an unknown amount with loose extras, and the expression must keep them separate.
hints: Try it with a made-up number first: if each bag held 10, how many buttons would you have, and how did you get it?
Whatever worked for 10 must be written so it works for any number in the box.
problems.socraticHint: What is the difference between three copies of the box and the box with three more thrown in?

variant.prompt: Every pack holds p pencils, the same number in each. You have 5 full packs and 3 loose pencils. Which expression counts all your pencils?

problems.prompt:
Priti checked whether 2n + 3 and 2(n + 3) are always equal.
Line 1: Try n = 4: 2n + 3 is 2 times 4 plus 3, which is 11.
Line 2: 2(n + 3) is 2 times (4 + 3), which is 2 times 7.
Line 3: 2 times 7 is 13.
Line 4: 11 does not equal 13, so 2n + 3 and 2(n + 3) are not always equal.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Lines 1 and 2 are correct: 2n + 3 at n = 4 is 11.
2(n + 3) at n = 4 is 2 times 7, but Line 3 is wrong: 2 times 7 is 14, not 13.
The corrected check still shows 11 does not equal 14, so Line 4's conclusion happens to still be true.
But Line 3's own arithmetic was wrong on the way there.
Do the inside first: adding 3 before multiplying by 2 gives a different total than multiplying by 2 first and adding 3 after.
That is exactly why the two expressions are not twins.
problems.useAgain: when a test value's own arithmetic needs checking on every line, even when the final conclusion sounds right.
hints: Recompute every line's own arithmetic yourself, even the ones that seem to be heading toward a correct-looking answer.
Break the pattern: a single test number can only expose an impostor if every step of the test is done correctly.
problems.socraticHint: Could a line's arithmetic be wrong even if the sentence right after it still sounds reasonable?

variant.prompt:
Owen checked whether 3(n + 2) and 3n + 2 are always equal.
Line 1: Try n = 5: 3(n + 2) is 3 times (5 + 2), which is 3 times 7.
Line 2: 3 times 7 is 21.
Line 3: 3n + 2 at n = 5 is 3 times 5 plus 2, which is 17.
Line 4: 21 does not equal 17, but since both sides used n = 5, they must be equal for every other number too.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: A balance scale sits perfectly level. The left pan holds 4 mystery boxes and 5 marbles. The right pan holds 1 mystery box and 23 marbles. Every box weighs the same. How many marbles is one box worth?
explanation: Keep the balance: do the same thing to both pans and the scale stays level.
Take away 1 mystery box from each pan: the left has 3 boxes and 5 marbles, the right has 23 marbles.
Take away 5 marbles from each pan: 3 boxes balance 18 marbles.
Share the 18 marbles evenly among the 3 boxes: one box is worth 6 marbles.
problems.useAgain: when boxes sit on both pans of a balance and you need to clear them from one side before solving.
hints: Remove the same number of boxes from both pans first, to get every box on one side.
Once only marbles remain on one side, remove matching marbles from both sides too.
problems.socraticHint: What can you remove from both pans at once without tipping the scale?

variant.prompt: A balance scale sits perfectly level. The left pan holds 5 mystery boxes and 3 marbles. The right pan holds 2 mystery boxes and 18 marbles. Every box weighs the same. How many marbles is one box worth?

problems.prompt: A balance scale sits perfectly level. The left pan holds 3 mystery boxes and 7 marbles. The right pan holds 5 mystery boxes and 1 marble. Every box weighs the same. How many marbles is one box worth?
explanation: Keep the balance: take away 3 mystery boxes from each pan.
The left pan now holds just 7 marbles, and the right holds 2 boxes and 1 marble.
Take away 1 marble from each pan: 6 marbles balance 2 boxes.
Share the 6 marbles evenly between the 2 boxes: one box is worth 3 marbles.
problems.useAgain: when boxes sit on both pans with different marble counts and you need to move them to one side first.
hints: Remove the smaller number of boxes from both pans, so boxes end up on only one side.
Once boxes sit on only one side, clear the marbles the same way.
problems.socraticHint: Which side has fewer boxes, and what happens if you remove that many boxes from both pans?

variant.prompt: A balance scale sits perfectly level. The left pan holds 2 mystery boxes and 9 marbles. The right pan holds 6 mystery boxes and 1 marble. Every box weighs the same. How many marbles is one box worth?

problems.prompt: A number n slides 6 steps down the number line and lands exactly on 9. What is n?
explanation: The story says n take 6 lands on 9.
Undo the slide: start at 9 and walk the 6 steps back up.
9 + 6 is 15, so n is 15. Check: 15 slide down 6 lands on 9.
problems.useAgain: when an unknown went through one move and you know where it landed, so undoing the move walks you home.
hints: The landing spot is known. The mystery is where the slide started.
Whatever a slide down does, the walk back up undoes.
problems.socraticHint: What single move undoes sliding 6 steps down, and why does undoing it from the landing spot find the start?

variant.prompt: A number m slides 8 steps down the number line and lands exactly on 14. What is m?

problems.prompt: The sentence x + 3 > 10 says: x plus 3 is bigger than 10. True or false: putting 7 in the box x makes the sentence true.
explanation: Put 7 in the box: 7 + 3 is 10.
The sentence demands bigger than 10, and 10 is not bigger than itself: a tipped scale must actually tip, and equal pans sit level.
So 7 makes the two sides exactly equal, which is precisely the one thing bigger-than refuses to count.
The first number that works is 8, one step past the balance point.
problems.useAgain: when a bigger-than sentence needs checking right at the edge, where equal and bigger part ways.
hints: Work out what the left side becomes when x is 7.
Now read the sentence strictly: does the left side beat 10, or only tie it?
problems.socraticHint: What is the difference between a scale that tips to one side and a scale that sits level, and which one does the bigger-than sign describe?

variant.prompt: The sentence y + 5 > 12 says: y plus 5 is bigger than 12. True or false: putting 8 in the box y makes the sentence true.

problems.prompt: What is the smallest whole number n that makes n + 4 > 11 true?
explanation: First find the balance point: n + 4 equals 11 exactly when n is 7.
At the balance point the scale sits level, and bigger-than needs it tipped, so 7 itself does not count.
One whole step past the balance point is 8, and 8 + 4 is 12, which beats 11.
Every whole number from 8 upwards works; 8 is the smallest.
problems.useAgain: when an inequality asks for its edge, and the answer sits one step past the value that makes both sides equal.
hints: Start by finding the n that makes the two sides exactly equal.
Decide whether the equal spot itself counts, then step along the number line accordingly.
problems.socraticHint: The equal spot and the answer are neighbours. What rule of the bigger-than sign pushes the answer off the equal spot?

variant.prompt: What is the smallest whole number m that makes m + 6 > 15 true?

problems.prompt: An inequality's answers get drawn on a number line like this: a circle marks the edge number, filled in if that number itself counts and hollow if it does not, and the line is shaded over all the numbers that work. On one drawing, a hollow circle sits on 5 and the shading runs to the right of it. Which inequality was drawn?
options: x is greater than or equal to 5
explanation: Shading to the right covers the numbers bigger than the circle, because right means bigger on the number line.
The circle is hollow, so 5 itself is left out of the club.
Bigger than 5, with 5 not included, is exactly x is greater than 5.
A filled circle would have let 5 in, and that is the whole difference between greater-than and greater-than-or-equal.
problems.useAgain: when a number line drawing must be read back into words, and the circle's fill decides whether the edge number joins in.
hints: Read the shading first: which side of the circle holds the numbers that work?
Then read the circle itself: does hollow let the edge number in, or shut it out?
problems.socraticHint: Why does the drawing need two different kinds of circle at all? What question about the edge number is the fill answering?

variant.prompt: On another number line drawing, a filled circle sits on 3 and the shading runs to the right of it. Which inequality was drawn?
options: x is greater than or equal to 3

steps.title: A triangle built from one length, and chances from a single die

problems.prompt:
Construct an equilateral triangle on segment AB, 6 cm long:
1. Open your compass to the exact length of AB.
2. Draw an arc centered at A.
3. Keeping the same compass width, draw an arc centered at B, crossing the first arc.
4. Join that crossing point to A and to B.
What is the length, in cm, of the two new sides you just drew?
explanation: Both arcs were drawn with the compass set to the exact same width as AB, and never changed.
That means the crossing point is exactly 6 cm from A and exactly 6 cm from B.
So both new sides are 6 cm long, the same as AB, which is why the triangle is equilateral.
problems.useAgain: when a compass width is set once and never changed, so every arc drawn with it marks points the exact same distance from its center.
hints: What compass width was used for both arcs?
Both new sides are exactly that same width, since the crossing point never moved off either arc.
problems.socraticHint: If the compass width never changed while drawing either arc, can the two new sides be different lengths from AB?

variant.prompt: The same construction is done on a segment 9 cm long. What is the length, in cm, of the two new sides?

problems.prompt: An equilateral triangle is constructed this way on a side 5 cm long. What is the triangle's perimeter, in cm?
explanation: All three sides of an equilateral triangle built this way are equal, each 5 cm.
Perimeter adds up all three sides: 5 plus 5 plus 5.
5 plus 5 plus 5 is 15 cm.
problems.useAgain: when every side of a shape built by this construction is known to be equal, and a total like perimeter is asked for.
hints: How many sides does this triangle have, and how long is each one?
Add all three equal sides together.
problems.socraticHint: If one side of the construction is 5 cm, does that tell you anything about the other two sides?

variant.prompt: An equilateral triangle is constructed this way on a side 8 cm long. What is the triangle's perimeter, in cm?

problems.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of rolling a prime number?
explanation: The prime numbers on a die are 2, 3 and 5, which is 3 out of the 6 faces.
3 out of 6 simplifies to 1/2.
problems.useAgain: when a single die's probability needs counting the faces that fit a rule, out of all 6.
hints: Which of the numbers 1 through 6 are prime?
Count those faces and put that count over 6.
problems.socraticHint: Is the number 1 a prime number, and does it belong in your count?

variant.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of rolling a multiple of 3?

problems.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of rolling a number less than 3?
explanation: Numbers less than 3 on a die are 1 and 2, which is 2 out of 6 faces.
2 out of 6 simplifies to 1/3.
problems.useAgain: when a die's probability rule is a range of numbers rather than a single value.
hints: Which numbers on the die count as less than 3?
Count those faces and put that count over 6, then simplify.
problems.socraticHint: Does less than 3 include the number 3 itself?

variant.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of rolling a number greater than 4?

steps.title: Primes are the atoms, and the dots come back

problems.prompt: Seven friends pass messages only between people who know each other's number directly. Ann knows Bo and Cy. Bo also knows Cy and Dee. Cy also knows Ellis. Dee also knows Fay. Ellis also knows Fay. Fay also knows Gus. Working layer by layer, everyone one hop from Ann, then everyone one more hop, and so on, what is the fewest hops for a message to travel from Ann to Gus?
explanation: Layer by layer: start at Ann and find everyone exactly one hop away first. That is Bo and Cy.
From Bo and Cy, find everyone new exactly one hop further. Bo reaches Dee, and Cy reaches Ellis, so Dee and Ellis are two hops from Ann.
From Dee and Ellis, the only new friend one hop further is Fay, who both of them know, so Fay is three hops from Ann.
Fay is the only friend who knows Gus, so Gus sits one hop past Fay. That makes four hops from Ann in all, for example Ann, Bo, Dee, Fay, Gus.
problems.useAgain: when you need the fewest hops between two dots in a network and want to be sure no shorter path exists.
hints: Do not search for a path from Ann to Gus straightaway. First find everyone exactly one hop from Ann.
Use each new layer to build the next one: anyone freshly reached this round unlocks new people one hop further next round.
problems.socraticHint: Once you know everyone exactly two hops from Ann, how do you decide who belongs in the very next layer?

figure.alt: A network of seven friends drawn as dots and lines. Ann connects to Bo and Cy. Bo also connects to Cy and Dee. Cy also connects to Ellis. Dee connects to Fay. Ellis connects to Fay. Fay connects to Gus. A message must travel along the lines from Ann to Gus.

variant.prompt: Seven computers pass data only along direct cables. Computer 1 connects to 2 and 3. Computer 2 also connects to 3 and 4. Computer 3 also connects to 5. Computer 4 also connects to 6. Computer 5 also connects to 7. Computer 6 also connects to 7. Working layer by layer, what is the fewest cables data must cross to get from computer 1 to computer 7?

problems.prompt: Every road on a map touches exactly two towns, one at each end, the same way every handshake involves exactly two people. If you visit each town and count how many roads touch it, that town's degree, then add up every town's degree, you count each road twice, once from each end. A network of 5 towns has degrees 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2. How many roads does the network have in total?
explanation: Handshake counting: adding up every town's degree counts every road exactly twice, once from each side. That is the same way counting who shook hands with whom counts every handshake twice.
Add the five degrees: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 is 12.
That total counted every road twice, so the real number of roads is half of it: 12 divided by 2 is 6.
problems.useAgain: when you know every dot's degree and need the total number of lines, since adding all the degrees always counts each line twice.
hints: Add up all five degrees first, without worrying about roads yet.
Remember that total counts every road twice, once from each end, so it is not the final answer yet.
problems.socraticHint: Why must the sum of every town's degree always come out as an even number?

variant.prompt: A network of 6 rooms has degrees 4, 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2. How many doors connect the rooms in total?

problems.prompt: Five friends stand in a circle: Ann next to Bo, Bo next to Cy, Cy next to Dee, Dee next to Ellis, and Ellis next to Ann, closing the ring. No two friends who stand next to each other may wear the same color shirt. What is the fewest colors needed so the rule is never broken?
explanation: Two colors or a cycle: try just 2 colors first, alternating around the ring. Go color 1, color 2, color 1, color 2, and so on.

Ann, Bo, Cy and Dee land on colors 1, 2, 1, 2, in that order. Ellis needs the opposite of Dee's 2, so color 1 is next. But Ellis also touches Ann, who is already color 1, so the ring closes on a clash.
That clash always happens in any ring with an odd number of friends. Alternating colors flip back and forth, and an odd loop can never flip back to where it started.
Give Ellis a third color instead: Ann is 1, Bo is 2, Cy is 1, Dee is 2, and Ellis is 3 this time. Three colors is enough, and two never can be for an odd ring.
problems.useAgain: when you need to know if two groups are enough for a network, since an odd loop in it always means they are not.
hints: Try coloring the ring with just 2 colors, alternating as you go around, and see what happens when you reach the last friend.
Count how many friends are in the ring. Does that count split evenly into alternating pairs, or is there one left over?
problems.socraticHint: Why does going around an odd number of friends in alternating colors always bring you back to clash with where you started?

variant.prompt: Six friends stand in a circle: Pam next to Quinn, Quinn next to Ravi, Ravi next to Sam, Sam next to Tia, Tia next to Uma, and Uma next to Pam, closing the ring. No two neighbors may wear the same color shirt. What is the fewest colors needed?

problems.prompt: Grow a factor tree for 84: split it into two factors, then keep splitting every branch that is not prime, until every branch ends on a prime leaf. Count the prime leaves, repeats included. How many leaves does the tree have?
explanation: One way down: 84 splits into 2 x 42, 42 splits into 2 x 21, and 21 splits into 3 x 7 total. Everything left is prime.
The leaves are 2, 2, 3 and 7, and indeed 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 is 84. Four leaves.
Here is the atoms promise at work: start differently, and say 84 as 4 x 21 this time. The 4 still splits into 2 x 2, landing on the exact same four leaves.
Every road down the tree ends at the same bag of atoms, because every number is built from primes in exactly one way.
problems.useAgain: when a number needs breaking into its atoms, and any split you can spot is a fine first move because all roads end the same.
hints: Any true split works as a start: 84 is even, so 2 goes into it cleanly.
A branch is only finished when the number on it is prime; anything else must split again.
problems.socraticHint: Two friends start the tree differently, one with 2 x 42 and one with 6 x 14. What do you expect at the bottom of their trees, and why?

variant.prompt: Grow a factor tree for 120 until every branch ends on a prime leaf. Counting repeats, how many prime leaves does it have?

problems.prompt: Factors usually come in pairs, which is why most numbers have an even count of factors: 24 had 8 of them. Yet a few special numbers have an odd count. What is the smallest number bigger than 1 with an odd number of factors?
explanation: Check the small numbers: 2 has factors 1 and 2, an even count. 3 has 1 and 3, even again.
4 has factors 1, 2 and 4: three factors, an odd count. Found it.
The reason is worth keeping: in the pair hunt for 4, the partner of 2 is 2 itself, because 2 x 2 is 4. A pair whose two members are the same person only counts one factor, so one pair collapses.
That only happens when some factor times itself makes the number, so the numbers with an odd count are exactly the squares. Tuck this away: it comes back to unlock a monster later this season.
problems.useAgain: when a factor count comes out odd, and that oddness is a square quietly announcing itself.
hints: List the factors of 2, then 3, and keep going, counting each list, until one count comes out odd.
When a pair's two partners turn out to be the same number, look closely at what that did to the count.
problems.socraticHint: Every factor pair of a number multiplies to that number. What would a factor have to be like to be its own partner?

variant.prompt: After 4, what is the next number with an odd number of factors?

problems.prompt: Two claims about primes. Claim one: every prime bigger than 2 is odd. Claim two: every odd number bigger than 2 is prime. Which is right?
explanation: Claim one holds: an even number bigger than 2 has 2 as an extra factor, so it has more than two factors and cannot be prime. That forces every bigger prime to be odd.
Claim two is the same sentence flipped around, and flipping is where the trap lives. To break it you need just one odd number that is not prime.
There it is at 9: odd, but 3 x 3, so not prime. One counterexample and claim two is dead.
All primes past 2 live among the odds, but the odds are a big neighbourhood and primes are only some of the houses.
problems.useAgain: when a true sentence gets flipped around and offered back, and one hunted counterexample decides whether the flip survives.
hints: Test the two claims separately; being cousins does not make them equally true.
For claim two, walk the odd numbers up from 3 and interview each one about its factors.
problems.socraticHint: How many counterexamples does it take to sink a claim that says the word every, and how many examples would it take to prove one?

variant.prompt: Two claims. Claim one: every prime bigger than 5 ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9. Claim two: every number bigger than 5 ending in 1, 3, 7 or 9 is prime. Which is right?

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write for a friend who missed the whole week: two different factor trees for 84, one starting 2 x 42 and one starting 6 x 14, always end on the very same four prime leaves. Say what a prime is in your own words, one idea per sentence, and finish with the sentence that explains why every road down a factor tree has to end the same way.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Teach the balance move to a grown-up in under two minutes. Draw or set up a balance, show why taking the same amount off both pans keeps it level, then have them invent a mystery-box puzzle on the spot and solve it out loud while they watch.
